accroche: In 1932, a New York publisher arranges the customs seizure of his own book, so that it can finally be put on trial, and published.
contenu_vulgarise:
In April 1932, the lawyer Morris Ernst has a copy of James Joyce's *Ulysses*, banned from import into the United States for years, brought from Paris aboard the liner *Bremen*. On his instructions, Joyce's friend and secretary, Paul Léon, has stuffed the book with laudatory reviews, slipped between the pages and under the cover. Customs, though forewarned, lets the parcel through without seizing it: it is simply forwarded to the publisher Random House. Ernst must then carry the still-sealed package to the customs office himself and demand its confiscation. “Everyone brings one back; no one pays attention,” he is told at first, before they comply. That is exactly what Random House wanted.

## A Trial Manufactured to Be Won

Since 1922, *Ulysses* had circulated under the counter in the United States: the 1930 customs law forbids bringing in a work judged obscene, and no publisher dares to publish it officially. Cerf, cofounder of Random House, wants to settle the question once and for all and have the book put on trial. With Ernst, he therefore stages this setup so that the court is forced to examine, as evidence, the book and the laudatory reviews that accompany it.

The case bears a strange name: *United States v. One Book Called Ulysses*. The defendant is the seized object itself. The customs law in fact allows a proceeding directed against the goods, without any need to name a person to be convicted.

## The Woolsey Ruling

On December 6, 1933, Judge John M. Woolsey issued his decision. He had read the whole book, not only the incriminated passages, and consulted literary opinions. His conclusion fits in a single sentence that remains famous: the effect of *Ulysses* on the reader is “emetic in places, undoubtedly, but nowhere aphrodisiac.” He judges the book sincere, demanding, never complacent, and therefore not obscene. The government appeals, but in 1934 the court upholds the ruling, two votes to one.

## What It Shifts

Woolsey had not been content to say “this book is not shocking.” He had laid down a principle: a work is judged as a whole, on its real effect on an ordinary reader, not on isolated sentences, nor on the supposed effect they would have on the most impressionable reader imaginable. This shift in the criterion, from a handful of shocking words to the intention and coherence of the whole work, reopens in America the way to a whole literature that had been banned until then. It prepares, decades ahead of its time, the criteria that courts would later apply to judge what is art and what is not.

citation.texte: I do not detect anywhere the leer of the sensualist. [...] [W]hilst in many places the effect of Ulysses on the reader undoubtedly is somewhat emetic, nowhere does it tend to be an aphrodisiac.
citation.source: United States v. One Book Called “Ulysses”, 5 F. Supp. 182 (S.D.N.Y. 1933)

carte.idee: Joyce's Ulysses was banned from import into the United States. In 1932, the publisher Random House arranges its seizure by customs itself, to provoke a trial. In 1933, Judge Woolsey declares it not obscene: judged “as a whole,” not on isolated passages.

quiz.question: Why does the case bear the name “United States v. One Book Called Ulysses” rather than the name of Joyce or his publisher?
choix: Because Joyce refused to appear in person before an American court
Because Random House had asked for anonymity to avoid publicity around the trial
Because the customs law allowed a proceeding directed against the seized object itself, without targeting a person
Because the 1930 law forbade naming a foreign publisher in a judgment
quiz.explication: The customs seizure fell under an “in rem” proceeding: it targeted the imported goods, not their author or publisher. That is why the book itself appears as a party in the title, a peculiarity of the 1930 customs law, not a precaution taken by Joyce or Random House, nor a rule about foreign publishers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Bennett Cerf, cofounder of Random House, stage this setup with the lawyer Morris Ernst?
choix: To quietly have the 1930 customs law overturned
To obtain James Joyce's copyright for free
To force a trial that would settle the question once and for all
To draw the press's attention to the other books in the Random House catalog
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Since 1922, Ulysses had circulated under the counter in the United States and no publisher dared to publish it officially. Cerf wanted to settle the question once and for all and have the book put on trial, which meant provoking the seizure himself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the book get from Paris to the New York customs, according to the entry?
choix: It is sent by French diplomatic pouch, safe from any search
Paul Léon stuffs it with laudatory reviews and sends it on the liner Bremen
Joyce hands it personally to Ernst during a trip to London
It is printed clandestinely on American soil, without ever crossing the Atlantic
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On Ernst's instructions, Joyce's friend and secretary, Paul Léon, stuffs the book with laudatory reviews slipped between the pages and under the cover, before sending it from Paris aboard the liner Bremen.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What principle does Judge Woolsey's ruling establish for assessing whether a work is obscene?
choix: Judge the work on isolated sentences, without regard to the whole
Judge the work as a whole, on its real effect on an ordinary reader
Judge the work on the effect it would have on the most impressionable reader imaginable
Entrust the judgment of obscenity to a jury of readers rather than a judge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Woolsey lays down that a work is judged as a whole, on its real effect on an ordinary reader, not on isolated sentences nor on the supposed effect they would have on the most impressionable reader imaginable. This shift in the criterion reopens the way to a whole literature that had been banned until then.
